notes: EXAMPLE, provided as a format reference. A student holds a wrong mental model of how a while loop terminates, then resolves it themselves with an analogy. Note that most of this conversation is noise: the greeting, the thanks, and the restatement of the lesson topic are all deliberately present, because an agent that extracts from them is over-extracting and we want that to be visible. Note also the classmate's name — a second child's data should not end up in this student's record.

turns.tutor: Hey! Ready to look at loops today?

turns.student: yeah. my while loop just keeps going forever and i don't know why
turns.tutor: Let's look at it together. What do you expect to happen to `i` as this runs?

turns.student: it goes up each time until the list is done right? i thought that's how it stops
turns.tutor: That's the key question. A while loop doesn't watch the list — it only checks the condition you wrote. Is anything in your code changing `i`?
That's a common one. The loop only stops when the condition becomes false, and nothing is making that happen yet.

turns.student: ok i added i = i + 1 and it worked. it's like a clock hand, it only moves if something moves it
turns.tutor: That's a good way to put it. Nothing moves unless you move it.

turns.student: jayden said loops were easy and i felt dumb but this makes sense now
turns.tutor: You worked it out yourself — that's the part that matters.

grains.text: Believes a while loop terminates when the list is exhausted, rather than when its condition becomes false
Grasps loop increment when framed as a clock hand that only moves if something moves it
Compares own pace unfavourably to classmates
